home-remodeling.hero_sub: Whole-home remodeling for Ponce-Davis and High Pines: gut renovations, structural openings, new systems, impact windows. Licensed GC CGC1539072, every scope permitted through Miami-Dade County and supervised on site daily.
intro_paragraphs: Ponce-Davis and High Pines sit between Coral Gables and South Miami, one leafy unincorporated square mile where 1950s ranches share quiet streets with new estates on half-acre and acre lots. Owners here face a familiar fork: sell to the teardown market, or remodel a solid midcentury house into something that earns its address. We do the second one. PGX handles whole-home renovations off Red Road, Davis Road, and Ponce de Leon Road: opened floor plans, raised ceilings where structure allows, new systems throughout, and finishes that match the caliber of the street.

Because the neighborhood is unincorporated, permits do not go to Coral Gables or South Miami city hall; they go to Miami-Dade County's Department of Regulatory and Economic Resources, known as RER. That means county plan review, DERM involvement when work affects protected trees, and Miami-Dade product approvals for every impact window and door in this High-Velocity Hurricane Zone. Some streets marketed as High Pines actually sit inside South Miami city limits, so we confirm jurisdiction from your folio before a single sheet is drawn. It sounds tedious. It is. It is also why our inspections pass.

A whole-home remodel at this level runs on discipline, not improvisation. PGX works from a fixed written scope, sequences trades so your family is not living in a job site longer than promised, and keeps a supervisor on your property every working day. The streets here are quiet and private; our crews, staging, and deliveries are managed to keep them that way. From first estimate through final inspection and warranty you deal with one accountable team, backed by 20-plus years building in South Florida and more than 150 remodels and additions delivered, all of them permitted.

faqs.q: Who issues building permits in Ponce-Davis?
faqs.a: Miami-Dade County. Ponce-Davis and most of High Pines are unincorporated, so permits run through the county's Department of Regulatory and Economic Resources rather than Coral Gables or South Miami city hall. Plans are filed through the county's online portal and the trades are inspected by county inspectors. A few streets on the High Pines edge sit inside South Miami limits, which changes the process, so we confirm jurisdiction from your folio before designing anything.

faqs.q: Should we remodel our house or is it a teardown?
faqs.a: Depends on the bones. Plenty of 1950s Ponce-Davis ranches have solid foundations, generous footprints, and rooflines worth keeping; a full remodel gets you a new house inside the old envelope with less disruption than rebuilding. Some homes genuinely are past saving, and we will tell you so. We walk the structure, look at what you want to end up with, and give you a straight answer either way. Honesty is free.

faqs.q: How long does a whole-home remodel take in Miami-Dade?
faqs.a: Plan on design and county permitting taking a few months before construction, then roughly six months to a year of building for a full gut, depending on scope and structural work. We put the schedule in writing with the contract and update it as inspections clear. What we do not do is quote a fantasy timeline to win the job and renegotiate it later.

faqs.q: Can we live in the house during the remodel?
faqs.a: For a true whole-home gut, we recommend moving out; you will be happier and the work goes faster. For phased remodels we can sometimes keep a wing livable, sealed off with real dust barriers and a working bathroom. We will tell you honestly which situation yours is during the walk-through, before you commit to anything.

faqs.q: What does a high-end whole-home remodel cost here?
faqs.a: Less than tearing down and rebuilding, more than new counters and a coat of paint. Serious whole-home remodels in this neighborhood are six-figure to seven-figure projects depending on size, structure, and finish level. We are not the cheapest bid and do not try to be; we price the full scope in writing so the number you sign is the number you pay, absent changes you approve.

kitchen-remodeling.title: Kitchen Remodeling for Ponce-Davis & High Pines, Miami FL
kitchen-remodeling.meta_description: Custom kitchens for Ponce-Davis and High Pines homes: cabinetry, stone, islands, and Miami-Dade permits handled end to end. Estimates at (786) 273-2524.
kitchen-remodeling.h1: Kitchens built for the long table
kitchen-remodeling.hero_sub: Custom kitchen remodeling in Ponce-Davis and High Pines: cabinetry built to the millimeter, stone worth arguing over, and every electrical, gas, and plumbing change permitted with Miami-Dade County, supervised daily by a licensed general contractor.
intro_paragraphs: In Ponce-Davis the kitchen carries a bigger job than most rooms in Miami: it feeds households that host, on lots big enough that guests never want to leave. High Pines cottages from the fifties tend to hide small, closed-off kitchens that deserve better, while newer estates off Davis Road were built around open plans that can feel dated a decade in. Either way, owners remodel toward the same target: a working kitchen with real storage, serious appliances, and an island long enough for homework, catering trays, and Sunday dinner at the same time.

Kitchen remodeling in this unincorporated pocket is permitted through Miami-Dade County RER rather than a city building department, with electrical, plumbing, and mechanical work each reviewed at the county level. Relocating a gas range or moving appliances across the room triggers trade permits most homeowners never see coming; we file them as a matter of course. There is no design-review board scrutinizing your cabinet style here, a freedom Ponce-Davis owners enjoy quietly. The county cares that the work is safe and legal. We care that it is both, and also beautiful.

This neighborhood expects things done properly, and PGX obliges: a fixed written scope before demolition, dust protection that treats the rest of the house as off-limits, and a supervisor on site every day there is a crew. Cabinetry is custom, and counters are templated only after cabinets are set, because the sequence is how seams stay where you will never see them. One team handles design coordination, permits, construction, and warranty, so nobody ever gets to point at somebody else.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a kitchen remodel in Ponce-Davis?
faqs.a: If the project touches electrical, plumbing, gas, or walls, yes, and almost every real kitchen remodel does. Because this area is unincorporated, permits go through Miami-Dade County rather than a city building department. We prepare the drawings, file the trade permits, and schedule the inspections as part of the job, so the paperwork is our problem, not yours.

faqs.q: How long will a custom kitchen take?
faqs.a: Custom cabinetry drives the calendar: quality cabinet packages typically take a few months to fabricate, so we run design, permitting, and cabinet orders in parallel, then build in an organized burst instead of an open-ended crawl. Construction itself usually runs a couple of months for a full kitchen. We would rather give you a real date than a flattering one.

faqs.q: Can you open the kitchen to the living areas?
faqs.a: Usually, and it is the most requested change in fifties-era High Pines homes, where kitchens were built as sealed workrooms. Some of those walls are load-bearing, which means engineering, a beam, and county-approved structural drawings rather than a sawzall and optimism. We check what is holding the roof up first and price the opening accordingly.

faqs.q: Do you work with our designer or architect?
faqs.a: Either way works. Many Ponce-Davis clients come with an architect or kitchen designer already on board, and we build to their documents while flagging anything that will not survive contact with the county or the budget. If you are starting from zero, we bring design partners we trust and coordinate the whole thing under one contract.

faqs.q: Is there an HOA that has to approve our kitchen?
faqs.a: On most Ponce-Davis and High Pines streets, no; there is no homeowners association and no municipal design board, so an interior kitchen remodel answers only to Miami-Dade County permitting. Gated enclaves such as Stonegate set their own rules for contractor access and work hours, and we handle that registration and scheduling whenever it applies.

kitchen-remodeling.cta_sub: Show us the kitchen you cook in now and describe the one you deserve. Estimates are detailed, written, and explained, in English o en español.

bathroom-remodeling.meta_description: Primary bath renovations in Ponce-Davis and High Pines with marble, frameless glass, and waterproofing done right. Permitted work. Call (786) 273-2524.
bathroom-remodeling.hero_sub: Bathroom remodeling for Ponce-Davis and High Pines homes: primary suites, frameless showers, freestanding tubs, and the waterproofing underneath, built by a licensed and insured GC with every trade permitted through Miami-Dade County.
intro_paragraphs: Estate homes in Ponce-Davis rarely need more bedrooms; they need better bathrooms. High Pines houses from the fifties came with one modest bath per wing and tile that has outlived three owners, and even newer construction near Schoolhouse Road often carries builder-grade primary baths that undersell the rest of the home. Owners here renovate toward the full suite: a frameless shower or true wet room, a freestanding tub that gets used, double vanities in stone, and storage planned like furniture instead of an afterthought.

Bathroom projects in this unincorporated enclave are permitted and inspected by Miami-Dade County under RER, covering the plumbing, the electrical, and any structural changes. Moving a drain in a 1950s slab means saw-cutting concrete and re-piping correctly, not improvising around cast iron that is quietly rusting from the inside; the county inspects that work before it is buried, and so do we. If your street happens to sit on the South Miami side of the boundary, the permit path changes, which is why we verify jurisdiction from the folio before design starts.

We treat waterproofing as the actual product and the marble as the reward for doing it right. Showers get full membrane systems, flood-tested before tile goes on: details no one will ever see and no one should ever have to think about again. PGX runs bathroom work with a fixed written scope, floor-to-ceiling protection along the path from front door to work zone, and daily supervision, because a remodel inside an occupied Ponce-Davis home should be an inconvenience, not an occupation. One licensed team carries it from estimate to warranty.

faqs.q: Are permits required for bathroom remodels in this area?
faqs.a: Yes, whenever plumbing, electrical, or structural work is involved, which covers essentially any bathroom remodel worth doing. Ponce-Davis is unincorporated, so permits are filed with Miami-Dade County and the work is inspected by county inspectors. Permitted work protects you at resale, and it keeps everyone honest about what is behind the tile. We file everything and we build it to pass the first time.

faqs.q: Can you relocate a shower or toilet on a concrete slab?
faqs.a: Yes. It means saw-cutting the slab, re-routing drains, and pouring back properly, which is routine for us and a disaster for the unlicensed. In fifties-era houses we often find original cast iron corroding from the inside; while the floor is open is the time to replace it. The county inspects the new plumbing before we close anything up.

faqs.q: How long does a primary bath renovation take?
faqs.a: Once permits are in hand and materials are on site, a full primary bathroom typically runs a couple of months of construction, longer if we are moving walls or combining rooms into a suite. Stone and glass lead times are the usual wildcard, so we order early and never demo your only working bathroom until the schedule is real.

faqs.q: What separates a high-end bathroom remodel from a standard one?
faqs.a: Mostly what you cannot see. Full waterproofing membranes flood-tested before tile, plumbing roughed to the millimeter so the drain sits centered, walls flattened so large-format slabs read as one surface, and ventilation sized for Miami humidity. The visible upgrades, the stone and frameless glass and custom vanities, only look right when the invisible work was done right first.

faqs.q: We live in a gated section. How do your crews operate?
faqs.a: Quietly, and on the association's terms. For gated pockets like Stonegate we register the crew, schedule deliveries in agreed windows, and keep the site contained and broom-clean. On the open streets of Ponce-Davis there is no association watching, so we hold ourselves to the same standard anyway. Your neighbors should know we were there from the result, not the noise.

home-additions.meta_description: Room additions and second stories on Ponce-Davis estate lots. Engineering, Miami-Dade County permits, daily supervision. Call PGX at (786) 273-2524.
home-additions.h1: Room to grow, no teardown required
home-additions.hero_sub: Home additions across Ponce-Davis and High Pines: rear extensions, second stories, and in-law suites engineered to current code, permitted through Miami-Dade County, and supervised every working day under license CGC1539072.
home-additions.local_heading: Acre lots were made for this
intro_paragraphs: Ponce-Davis lots run from half an acre to well over an acre, which means most owners who need space do not need to move; they need a contractor who can add it. Families here stretch 1950s ranches with rear wings and new primary suites, put second stories on homes near Red Road and Sunset Drive, and convert garages into gyms, offices, and in-law quarters. With Gulliver, Epiphany, and St. Thomas Episcopal minutes away, this is a neighborhood people settle into for decades. The houses have to keep up.

Additions in unincorporated Miami-Dade go through county RER review: a zoning check on setbacks and lot coverage, full structural plan review, and a DERM tree permit if the footprint forces a protected oak to be removed or relocated. New foundations must tie correctly into old ones, and tie beams often need upgrading before a second story is even a conversation; our engineers design for that, and the county verifies it. Ponce-Davis has no municipal design board, but the inspectors read plans carefully. So do we.

An addition done right should read as original to the house: the same floor level, matched roof lines, stucco that does not telegraph the seam. PGX carries the full chain of survey, engineering, county permits, construction, and finish work under one fixed written scope, with a supervisor on the property daily and staging that respects a quiet street. You keep living in the house while we build. We keep the site contained, the schedule honest, and the paperwork airtight from estimate through warranty.

faqs.q: How large an addition does zoning allow on my lot?
faqs.a: Unincorporated Miami-Dade zoning sets the setbacks and lot coverage, and on Ponce-Davis estate lots those limits usually leave far more room than owners expect. The honest answer requires pulling your folio, checking the zoning district, and running the numbers on your survey, which we do before design begins so nobody falls in love with an addition the county will never approve.

faqs.q: Will we need tree permits for the addition?
faqs.a: Possibly. The oak and banyan canopy is a defining feature of Ponce-Davis, and in unincorporated Miami-Dade removing or relocating a protected tree requires a permit through the county's environmental division, DERM. Our first move is designing the footprint around significant trees, which usually works on lots this size. When removal is unavoidable, we handle the permitting and any required mitigation.

faqs.q: Is an addition smarter than tearing down and rebuilding?
faqs.a: In Ponce-Davis both happen constantly, so it is a fair question. If the existing structure is sound and the layout mostly works, an addition delivers the space with less money, less time, and less disruption, and you keep what you like about the house. If the house fights you at every turn, rebuilding can win. We will run both scenarios with you honestly.

faqs.q: How long does a home addition take from start to finish?
faqs.a: Budget several months for survey, engineering, and Miami-Dade County plan review before ground breaks, then roughly four to nine months of construction depending on whether it is a single-room extension or a full second story. Structural reviews are thorough here, and we would rather clear them properly than rush a set of plans that bounces back twice.

faqs.q: Can we live at home while you build the addition?
faqs.a: Usually, yes; that is one of the underrated advantages of adding instead of rebuilding. We keep the existing house sealed and functional while the new structure goes up outside, and we schedule the tie-in, the phase where we open the wall between old and new, as a tightly managed sprint rather than a months-long hole in your home.

outdoor-living.title: Outdoor Living Builders for Ponce-Davis Estates, Miami FL
outdoor-living.meta_description: Summer kitchens, terraces, and pergolas for Ponce-Davis acre lots, designed and county-permitted by PGX Builders Group. Estimates: call (786) 273-2524.
outdoor-living.h1: The backyard is the whole point
outdoor-living.hero_sub: Outdoor living construction for Ponce-Davis and High Pines estates: terraces, summer kitchens, pergolas, and driveways, built by a licensed general contractor with Miami-Dade County permits and daily on-site supervision.
intro_paragraphs: Nobody buys an acre in Ponce-Davis to admire it through a window. Life here is built around the outdoors: morning coffee under the oaks, dinner for twenty on the terrace, kids and dogs with real room to run. Owners invest accordingly, in covered loggias with summer kitchens, pergolas over stone terraces, pools framed in travertine, and driveways that can absorb a school-morning shuttle and a Saturday party without flinching. High Pines yards run smaller but work harder, and we design for both.

Outdoor structures in this unincorporated corner of Miami-Dade are permitted through the county's RER, from footings for pergolas to gas and electric for summer kitchens to drainage for new driveways. The tree canopy is part of the deal: removing or relocating a protected oak requires a DERM permit, so we design terraces around trees rather than through them. And because most streets here have no HOA design committee, what gets built is between you, your architect, and the county. That is a freedom worth using well.

PGX builds exteriors with the same discipline as interiors: fixed written scope, real drawings, daily supervision, and trades who understand that an established garden is not a staging yard. We coordinate re-roofs, stucco, and exterior paint alongside outdoor construction so the house and grounds finish as one project instead of three overlapping ones. Every gas line, footing, and outlet is permitted and inspected, because a summer kitchen should outlast the trends it was designed around. That is the only way we build.

scope_items.desc: Stucco repair, full repaints, impact window and door openings, and re-roof coordination timed to finish with the rest of the project.

faqs.q: Does a summer kitchen or pergola need a permit here?
faqs.a: Almost always. Footings, roofed structures, gas lines, and electrical circuits all require permits, and in Ponce-Davis those run through Miami-Dade County because the area is unincorporated. Unpermitted outdoor structures have a way of surfacing during appraisals and sales, usually at the worst possible moment. We permit everything we build, which is exactly why we are comfortable standing behind it.

faqs.q: Can you build the terrace around our existing oaks?
faqs.a: That is our preference. Protected trees in unincorporated Miami-Dade fall under county rules enforced through DERM, and mature canopy is a large part of what makes these lots worth what they are worth. We design terraces, pergolas, and driveways around root zones and drip lines, and when a tree genuinely must come out, we secure the permit rather than gamble with a chainsaw.

faqs.q: Do you build pools too?
faqs.a: We build everything around the pool: terraces, coping, summer kitchens, pergolas, equipment enclosures, and the drainage that keeps water where it belongs. Pool shells themselves are specialty-licensed work, so we coordinate with an established pool contractor and fold their schedule into ours. You get one integrated backyard project instead of three contractors pointing at each other.

faqs.q: How disruptive is outdoor construction to the property?
faqs.a: Less than you would fear when it is planned. We define access routes and staging areas before work starts, protect existing landscaping and hardscape along the path, and keep equipment off everything that is not in the scope. Streets in Ponce-Davis are quiet and private, and our job sites are run to match them.

faqs.q: What should we budget for a summer kitchen and terrace?
faqs.a: It varies with size, stone, and appliances more than anything else. A built-in grill under an existing cover is one conversation; a full outdoor kitchen with refrigeration, gas, stone counters, and a new pergola over a travertine terrace is another. As a high-end contractor we will not be the lowest number, but the scope is fixed in writing and the work is permitted, inspected, and warrantied.

outdoor-living.cta_sub: Walk the yard with us. We will sketch what fits, flag what needs permits, and price it straight, in English o en español.
